title: Tier III Checkpoint I — An Advanced Unit

points.h: Ground It in Discourse and Pragmatics
pts: Choose a unit theme rich enough to support explicit cohesion, coherence and pragmatic-competence work, not just vocabulary and grammar.
Build in at least one dedicated pragmatics focus — a speech act, a politeness strategy — relevant to the unit's communicative goal.
Plan a coherence-diagnosis activity using a deliberately flawed model text.

v: Scheme of work (Unit 14); three candidate themes

items: List three possible themes for a four-to-six-week unit.
For each, ask: does it offer a text type with clear cohesion and coherence features (Unit 52)? Does it offer a real speech act, such as complaining, requesting or proposing (Unit 53)?
Choose the theme that scores best, and name one pragmatics focus.
Write, or adapt, a model text containing deliberate coherence problems for a diagnosis activity.
Plan where the diagnosis activity will sit in the unit.
In a DIET workshop, groups plan the same theme for different levels and compare.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: The Water in Our City plan (written for this book):

lines: Pragmatic focus: complaining and proposing politely to an authority (indirect requests, hedging, acknowledging the reader’s position).
Coherence diagnosis: a letter in which the complaint appears only in the final paragraph, and ‘however’ is used where no contrast exists.
T: What is the writer asking for, and when do we find out?
S1: Only at the end. The first three paragraphs are just history.
S2: And the ‘however’ in paragraph two is confusing. There is no contrast.

blocks.x: Such diagnosis makes coherence visible in a way that correcting sentences does not (Halliday and Hasan 1976).

body: Purpose: to show a rich theme supporting several strands. Content: a water tank cut away to show layers labelled ‘content’, ‘genre’, ‘speech act’, ‘coherence’ and ‘critical questions’. Style: clean cross-section. Board version: a rectangle divided into five horizontal bands.

items: Google Docs (free) for a shared unit-planning template.

blocks.x: A one-page planning grid photocopied for each teacher.

pts: Select a genre appropriate to the unit's aim and run the complete teaching-learning cycle — field-building through independent construction.
Resist the temptation to skip joint construction, even under time pressure — its bridging function is where this cycle earns its value.
Plan feedback calibrated to each stage of the cycle, not a single feedback approach throughout.

v: The unit timeline; a genre cycle planning sheet (Unit 54)

items: Place the five stages of the teaching-learning cycle on the unit timeline: building the context, modelling and deconstruction, joint construction, independent construction, and linking to related texts (Feez 1998).
Allocate lessons to each stage; protect at least one full lesson for joint construction.
For each stage, decide the main feedback approach (see model language).
Identify the model texts and where they come from.
Check the total time against the scheme of work.
In very large classes, run joint construction on the board with the whole class, then in groups of six with one scribe.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Feedback planned for each stage (written for this book):

lines: Building the context: questions and oral feedback on content knowledge; no language correction yet.
Modelling: feedback on learners’ analysis of stages and language features.
Joint construction: immediate, shared reformulation on the board.
Independent construction: written feedback against the genre criteria, with one conference per learner.

blocks.x: A teacher’s note: Last term I skipped joint construction to save time, and independent drafts were weak in exactly the moves we had not built together. Joint construction is the bridge between analysing a model and writing alone.

body: Purpose: to show a genre cycle mapped on to real lessons. Content: a four-week calendar with coloured blocks for each stage, and a padlock icon on the joint construction lesson. Style: tidy, practical. Board version: a grid of lessons with stage initials.

items: Google Sheets (free) for a colour-coded unit calendar.

blocks.x: A timeline drawn along the top of the board for the length of the unit.

body: When time runs short, shorten building the context or linking to related texts, not joint construction. Learners can research the field at home; they cannot easily learn to compose with the teacher unless it happens in class.

pts: Ask whether the unit's theme could sustain genuine content integration across several lessons, not just a single activity.
Where it can, map the 4Cs across the whole unit and plan dual content-and-language assessment.
This isn't mandatory for every unit, but worth deliberately evaluating given this tier's depth of CLIL methodology.

items: Ask whether the theme could sustain content learning across several lessons, not just one activity.
If yes, meet the relevant subject teacher (here, environmental science or geography).
Map the 4Cs across the whole unit: content, communication, cognition and culture.
Plan dual assessment: one criterion for content accuracy and one for language.
If no, note why, and keep content as context rather than integration.
Where a subject teacher is not available, use NCERT or state-board science textbook chapters as the content source.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: The 4Cs for Water in Our City (written for this book):

lines: Content: the urban water cycle; groundwater depletion; rainwater harvesting.
Communication: language of cause and effect (‘As a result…’, ‘This leads to…’); formal proposal language.
Cognition: evaluating solutions against cost and fairness.
Culture: traditional water systems, such as Bengaluru’s lakes and tanks, and community responsibility.

blocks.x: A CLIL angle is not compulsory for every unit, but it deserves deliberate evaluation (Coyle, Hood and Marsh 2010).

body: Purpose: to show the 4Cs across a unit. Content: four overlapping circles labelled content, communication, cognition and culture, with short examples from the water unit in each, and the unit title at the centre. Style: clean Venn diagram. Board version: four overlapping circles.

items: NCERT e-textbooks via the ePathshala portal (free) for subject content.

blocks.x: Printed textbook chapters shared by the subject teacher.

pts: Offer at least one substantial choice point within the unit, formalised as a mini learning-contract for a specific sub-goal.
Schedule a brief advising check-in partway through, reviewing progress against that specific choice.
This connects the unit to each learner's broader ongoing autonomy development, not just this unit's content.

v: 20 minutes to set up; 5 minutes per learner midway

items: Identify one substantial choice point: for example, which local water problem to investigate and which sources to use.
Learners complete a mini contract for that sub-goal: problem chosen, sources, evidence, date.
Schedule a brief advising check-in at the midpoint of the unit.
At the check-in, the learner reports progress; the teacher asks and suggests but does not decide.
Link the contract to each learner’s wider autonomy record.
Learners working in pairs complete a shared contract with named responsibilities.
Support: offer three problems and three sources to choose from.
Challenge: learners include a primary source, such as an interview or a local survey.

blocks.x: A mini contract (written for this book):

lines: Sub-goal: investigate water supply in my apartment complex in Whitefield.
Sources: a resident association notice; an interview with the building manager in Kannada; one newspaper report.
Evidence: notes and a one-page summary in English by week 3.
T: How is the interview going?
S: He agreed, but only on Sunday.
T: Would that still leave you time to write the summary before week 3?

blocks.x: A single well-chosen choice point builds autonomy without overturning the unit’s structure (Holec 1981).

body: Purpose: to show a bounded choice point. Content: a path through the unit that branches briefly into three routes (different local problems) and rejoins before the final task. Style: simple map. Board version: a line that splits and rejoins.

items: Google Forms (free) for submitting mini contracts.

points.h: Design the Unit Test for Washback
pts: Before finalising the unit's content, ask what teaching behaviour the planned end-of-unit assessment will encourage.
Include genuinely communicative, task-based components in the test, not only discrete-item accuracy checks.
Pilot the assessment informally with a colleague or a small group before full deployment, if time allows.

items: Before finalizing lessons, draft the end-of-unit assessment.
Ask: if learners prepared only for this, what would they practise?
Make sure it includes task-based components: the letter and a short oral presentation of the proposal.
Keep discrete items (for example, cohesive devices in a gapped text) to a small share.
If time allows, pilot the assessment with a colleague or five learners and revise.
Share an intent note with learners at the start: ‘This is what the assessment will reward.’
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Letter of complaint and proposal (50%): scored with a genre-specific rubric for stages, coherence, politeness and accuracy.
Oral presentation of the proposal, three minutes (30%): scored for organization, audience awareness and intelligibility.
Language in context (20%): a gapped letter testing cohesive devices and hedging.

blocks.x: Its washback: learners practise real letters and proposals rather than memorizing a format. Designing the test first makes washback a design choice (Alderson and Wall 1993).

body: Purpose: to show backward design. Content: a path of lessons leading to a finish line where the assessment sits; an arrow loops back from the finish to the start, labelled ‘what will this encourage?’. Style: clean. Board version: a line with a flag and a curved arrow back.

items: Google Docs (free) for the assessment and its rubric, shared with colleagues.

blocks.x: A handwritten rubric displayed during the unit.

points.h: Verify Key Language With Corpus Data
pts: Check at least one key structure or collocation planned for explicit teaching against real corpus evidence.
Source one or two authentic example sentences directly from concordance lines for the unit's materials.
This habit, repeated across units, steadily improves the evidence base behind a teacher's everyday materials.

v: A corpus tool (Unit 58); the unit’s language focus list

items: Choose one structure or collocation you will teach explicitly.
Check it in a corpus: frequency, typical collocates and register.
Adjust your explanation if the evidence differs from the coursebook.
Select one or two concordance lines as authentic examples for the unit worksheet, lightly edited.
Add the finding to your corpus log.
Ask C1 learners to carry out the check themselves and report.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A teacher’s check for the unit (written for this book):

lines: Question: Is ‘water scarcity’ or ‘water shortage’ more usual?
Finding: both are common; ‘scarcity’ appears more in academic and policy writing, ‘shortage’ in news and everyday use. [VERIFY with a corpus search before teaching]
Decision: use ‘shortage’ in the complaint letter and ‘scarcity’ in the formal proposal section.
Also checked: ‘complain about’ (not ‘complain on’) and ‘request that the council…’.

blocks.x: Repeated across units, this small habit steadily improves the evidence behind everyday materials (O’Keeffe, McCarthy and Carter 2007).

body: Purpose: to show a brief corpus check within planning. Content: a planning sheet with one phrase circled, a magnifying glass over two short concordance lines, and a tick beside the revised explanation. Style: practical. Board version: a phrase, two lines of examples and a tick.

items: SkELL (free) or English-Corpora.org (free with registration; limits).

blocks.x: A learner dictionary and a collocation dictionary.

pts: Audit the unit's materials briefly for whose culture and whose variety of English they centre.
Where relevant, build in explicit discussion of language variety or cultural perspective as part of the unit's content, not just its subtext.
This doesn't require rewriting the unit — a brief, conscious audit is often enough to catch avoidable blind spots.

v: Teacher activity; B2–C1 learners for step 4

items: Ask of the materials: whose voices and circumstances are centred? Whose are missing?
Ask: which variety of English is modelled, and is any local usage treated as wrong without reason?
Add one text or task that fills a gap you found.
Where relevant, plan a short class discussion as part of the unit’s content, not only its subtext.
Note the change in the unit plan.
Learners audit one text themselves and suggest whose voice to add.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Findings for Water in Our City (written for this book):

lines: Centred: apartment residents writing to the city council.
Missing: residents of informal settlements who depend on public taps and tankers.
Added: a short interview with a community worker (written for this book) and a discussion question: ‘Who suffers most from water shortages, and whose complaints are heard?’
Variety: ‘tanker’, ‘borewell’ and ‘sump’ are established Indian English words; use them without apology, and gloss them for outside readers.

blocks.x: A brief, conscious audit is often enough to catch avoidable blind spots (Fairclough 1992).

body: Purpose: to prompt the critical questions. Content: a queue at a public tap, with speech bubbles from different residents, and a letter to the council in the foreground that includes some voices and not others. Style: respectful, realistic. Board version: a line of stick figures and a letter.

items: Padlet (free plan, limited boards) for learners to post voices they would add.

blocks.x: Slips of paper on which learners write one missing voice.

points.h: Close and Reflect at Tier III Depth
pts: End the unit with reflection addressing discourse, pragmatic, genre and autonomy dimensions, not just linguistic accuracy.
Log what worked at this greater methodological depth for the next unit in the sequence, continuing Unit 9's reflective cycle.
This single unit is the model Units 61 onward will build further specialisation on top of.

v: A reflection sheet; the teacher’s planning log

items: Learners complete a reflection with four prompts: coherence, politeness, genre and managing their own sub-goal.
In groups, they share one thing they can now do and one they still find hard.
The teacher collects the sheets and notes patterns.
The teacher logs what worked, what did not, and one change for the next unit (Unit 9).
File the unit plan, assessment, log and learner reflections together as a model for later units.
Learners write the reflection as a short letter to next year’s class.
Support: sentence starters for each prompt.
Challenge: learners set a new sub-goal for the next unit based on their reflection.

blocks.x: Learner reflection prompts and one response (written for this book):

lines: Coherence: I now put my main request in the first paragraph.
Politeness: I learnt to say ‘We would be grateful if…’ instead of ‘You must…’.
Genre: I know the stages of a proposal.
My sub-goal: the interview was hard to arrange; next time I will start in week 1.

blocks.x: Teacher’s log: Joint construction worked well; the oral presentation needed one more rehearsal lesson. Next unit (Unit 61, academic writing) will build on the proposal stages.

body: Purpose: to show reflection across four dimensions. Content: four small mirrors labelled coherence, politeness, genre and autonomy, each reflecting a different part of a learner’s letter. Style: warm, clear. Board version: four squares with labels.

items: Google Forms (free) for the reflection; Google Drive (free) for filing the complete unit.

blocks.x: A reflection sheet and a box file for the unit.

body: Plan your next advanced unit using the eight checks in this unit. You do not need to include everything: note beside each check whether you used it, adapted it or decided against it, and why. Teach the unit, then review your notes with a colleague.

dek: Unit 60 of 100: closing the opening stretch of Tier III by designing one advanced-level unit that draws Units 51 through 59 together into a single piece of real planning.

aims.x: This checkpoint closes the opening stretch of Part III. Units 51–59 each examined one area of advanced pedagogy in depth: discourse, pragmatics, genre, CLIL, autonomy, washback, corpus evidence and critical awareness. Specialist knowledge proves its value only when it is combined in real planning. This unit therefore works through the design of one advanced unit of four to six weeks, for learners at B2–C1, using a single running example. Each point applies one earlier unit, and the activities are planning tasks for teachers, teacher educators and DIET faculty.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: choose a unit theme rich enough to support discourse and pragmatics work as well as vocabulary and grammar;
plan a full genre teaching-learning cycle, including joint construction, with stage-appropriate feedback;
decide whether a unit can sustain genuine content integration, and map the 4Cs where it can;
build a mini learning contract and an advising check-in into a unit;
design an end-of-unit assessment with its washback in mind;
verify key language with corpus evidence and source authentic examples;
audit a unit briefly through a critical lens;
close a unit with reflection that covers discourse, pragmatics, genre and autonomy, and log lessons for the next unit.

why: Why this matters. Nine posters of specialist depth only prove useful combined. This checkpoint tests whether they cohere into one coherent, teachable C1-level unit.

background.x: Unit 10 and Unit 20 asked teachers to build a lesson and then a unit from Part I principles, and Unit 35 and Unit 45 did the same for integrated skills in Part II. The task now is harder, because the ingredients are more specialized. Cohesion and coherence (Halliday and Hasan 1976), politeness and speech acts (Brown and Levinson 1987), and the genre teaching-learning cycle (Feez 1998) each come with their own planning logic. CLIL brings the 4Cs framework of content, communication, cognition and culture (Coyle, Hood and Marsh 2010). Autonomy (Holec 1981), washback (Alderson and Wall 1993), corpus evidence (O’Keeffe, McCarthy and Carter 2007) and critical language awareness (Fairclough 1992) add further lenses. None of these needs to dominate a unit, but each should be considered deliberately.

The running example used throughout is a unit called Water in Our City, designed for a first-year undergraduate class or a Class 11 elective in Bengaluru, with about 45 learners at B2 and a few at C1. The communicative goal is to write a formal letter of complaint and proposal to a civic body about a local water problem, and to present the proposal orally. The theme connects with environmental science, with learners’ daily lives (tanker water, borewells, rainwater harvesting) and with questions of access and fairness. All details of the example are written for this book.

This design reflects national priorities. NEP 2020 calls for experiential, integrated and discussion-based learning, and for assessment that tests competencies (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020). NCF 2023 asks that language learning connect with learners’ lives and other subjects, and that learners’ languages be used as resources (NCERT 2023). Learners in the example may research in Kannada, Tamil or Urdu sources and interview family members in their home languages, then report in English. Reflective practice (Schön 1983; Unit 9) runs through the whole design: the unit is a hypothesis to be tested, not a script.

items: Unit plan. A complete plan for one advanced unit, showing how each of Units 52–59 was considered, used or set aside.
Genre cycle map. A timeline of the teaching-learning cycle with stage-specific feedback and protected joint construction.
Assessment with intent note. An end-of-unit assessment with a brief statement of its intended washback.
Reflective log. Learner reflections and a teacher log summarizing what to carry into the next unit.
Which of Units 52–59 was easiest to build into your unit, and which was hardest?
Where did time pressure tempt you to skip a stage, and what did you decide?
Did the CLIL decision change your unit, or confirm that integration was not suitable?
How did the mini contract affect learners’ engagement?
What did the critical audit reveal that you had not noticed before?
What will you carry forward into your next unit?

perm: The Water in Our City unit, including all model texts, contracts, assessments, dialogues, reflections and logs, is written for this book. Real newspaper reports, civic notices or textbook chapters used in the unit should be short extracts with sources given. Screenshots of Google tools, Padlet, SkELL or ePathshala require permission or replacement with original illustrations.

terms.def: A planning framework for CLIL that asks teachers to integrate content, communication, cognition and culture in each unit (Coyle, Hood and Marsh 2010); for example, a science lesson on the water cycle also plans its language and thinking demands.
Planning that begins with the intended outcomes, then decides how they will be assessed, and only then chooses activities (Wiggins and McTighe 2005); also called backward planning.
An analysis identifying why a learner text does not hang together, such as a main point that appears only at the end or a linking word used where no contrast exists.
A quick check of a word or phrase in a corpus before teaching it, to confirm how common and natural it is; for example, comparing I have a doubt with I have a question.
A brief review of a unit or material through a critical lens, asking whose voices, views and values are included or left out.
A stage of a genre teaching-learning cycle in which teacher and class write a text together, with the teacher thinking aloud about the writer’s decisions.

A written agreement, negotiated between learner and teacher, that sets out the learner’s goals, the activities and resources to be used, a timeline and how progress will be evaluated; a brief ‘mini’ version can be built into a single unit.
The genre-based cycle of building the field, deconstructing model texts, joint construction and independent construction, with support gradually reduced (Martin and Rose 2008).
The topic that holds a unit of work together, chosen to be rich enough to support discourse and pragmatics work as well as vocabulary and grammar.

The effect of a test on teaching and learning, which may be positive or negative (Alderson and Wall 1993). Board examinations that test only reading and writing often lead to neglect of listening and speaking.
